clue.text: Number of singers about fifty

definitions.note: read as 'something that numbs', not a figure

indicators.note: the singers' word goes round, wrapping about the Roman numeral

blocks.note: adjective for what a choir does, standing for the singers
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: A head count of a choir that comes to roughly fifty voices.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' looks like a quantity, but it is something that makes you numb.
explanation.definitionFit: Chloral is an old sedative drug that dulls sensation, so it is literally a thing which numbs.

clue.text: Look out from hiding-place?

blocks.note: first meaning: old schoolboy Latin warning, 'beware!'
second meaning: a hollow in a hillside

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests peeping from a hide; the Latin word for 'beware' was British school slang for a lookout's warning.
explanation.definitionFit: Cave, Latin for beware, was shouted by pupils keeping watch, and a cave is a hollow for hiding.

clue.text: Gunner with a stripe provides a cobbler with a minder

indicators.note: the following words provide the raw material, to be made over into a new order

explanation.surface: An artillery soldier offers a shoe-mender a bodyguard.
explanation.walkthrough: The joining 'with' sits inside the fodder, linking the two phrases whose letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A lance-bombardier is the lowest NCO rank in the British Royal Artillery, wearing a single chevron on the sleeve.

clue.text: Cure for extreme dyslexia

indicators.note: the cure is found sitting within the phrase that follows

blocks.note: end of the first word joined to the start of the second

explanation.surface: A treatment for a severe case of a reading difficulty.
explanation.definitionFit: A remedy is a treatment that heals an illness, so it is a cure.

clue.text: Don't punish the French gentleman

explanation.surface: A plea to spare a French gentleman from penalty.
explanation.walkthrough: A toff is British slang for an upper-class man.
explanation.definitionFit: To let someone off is to excuse them from a penalty, deciding against punishment.

clue.text: From orphan to mother - that's the spirit!

indicators.note: 'from ... to' marks off a stretch of the clue's own letters to lift out

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of orphan, all of to, and the start of mother

explanation.surface: Cheering on someone who has gone from being an orphan to being a mother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's the spirit!' reads as encouragement, but only its last word defines.
explanation.definitionFit: A phantom is a ghost or apparition, which is one common meaning of a spirit.

clue.text: Role call: solution, fiery exit line

explanation.surface: Theatre jargon: a role call, then a fiery closing line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Role call' plays on roll call. Parthian horsemen shot arrows back while riding away, hence a cutting remark on leaving.
explanation.definitionFit: A Parthian shot is a sharp parting remark, the kind of line delivered on exit.

clue.text: Promptitude, city style, to embrace the right

indicators.note: the town's word wraps its arms round the letter for right

blocks.note: à la, in the style of

explanation.surface: Speed in a cosmopolitan manner that takes in the political right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'À la' means 'in the style of', as in à la mode; the clue puts it after city though it comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: Alacrity is brisk, eager readiness, matching the old word for quickness in acting.

clue.text: It isn't given to us, they say: leave wooden bits out

definitions.text: It isn't given to us, they say

indicators.note: out as in out of place, so the letters are knocked into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A woodworking instruction to omit timber pieces, next to a proverb about gifts.
explanation.walkthrough: The saying, from Publilius Syrus via Bacon, is that it is impossible to love and be wise; the clue alludes to it.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb holds that no person is granted the ability both to adore someone and keep sound judgment.

clue.text: One delving below the surface without fear - a psychologist?

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the digger surrounds the fear

explanation.surface: A fearless explorer of the subconscious, possibly a psychologist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without fear' reads as 'fearless', but without means outside here. The question mark flags a psychologist as a playful example.
explanation.definitionFit: A psychologist might jokingly be thought to know people's thoughts, like a telepath who reads minds.

clue.text: Ecclesiastical title getting high honour is poison

blocks.note: short for Venerable, the title of an archdeacon
the Order of Merit, a top British honour

explanation.surface: A churchman receiving a great honour is said to be poisonous.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ven. is how an archdeacon is styled; the OM (Order of Merit) is a select honour given by the British monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Venom is the toxic fluid injected by snakes and spiders, a kind of poison.

clue.text: Exclusive physicist in water needs waterproof

definitions.note: used as a noun, a waterproof sheet

indicators.note: the scientist sits inside the stretch of water

blocks.note: Wolfgang Pauli, of the Pauli exclusion principle

explanation.surface: A snobbish scientist out in the rain wants a raincoat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exclusive' seems to mean snobbish but points to Pauli's exclusion principle.
explanation.definitionFit: A tarpaulin is a heavy tarred or coated canvas sheet used as a protective waterproof cover.

clue.text: Male has trouble with note about female model in first boat

indicators.note: the banknote is wrapped about the female and the model

explanation.surface: A man gets into a fuss over a woman who models.
explanation.walkthrough: A fiver is a five-pound note. In rowing bumps races, the crew finishing top is Head of the River.
explanation.definitionFit: Head of the River is the title held by the leading crew in college rowing races, the first boat.

clue.text: The big guns of rock

blocks.note: second meaning: a loud style of music

explanation.walkthrough: 'Big guns of rock' sounds like the stars of the music scene, but the two parts are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Large-calibre artillery was once called heavy metal, and the phrase also names a loud genre of rock music.

clue.text: Love is painful when wrongly directed

indicators.note: sent the wrong way, so the word is read from its end back to its start

explanation.surface: A proverb that love hurts when it is aimed at the wrong person.
explanation.walkthrough: Eros, the Greek god of love, stands for love itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Eros is the Greek god of desire, and the word is used for sexual or romantic love.

clue.text: Conclusive instructors of actors in film

blocks.note: the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art, a London drama school

explanation.surface: Drama teachers giving final notes to the cast of a movie.
explanation.walkthrough: RADA is London's best-known drama school.
explanation.definitionFit: La Strada is Federico Fellini's 1954 Italian movie about travelling street performers.

clue.text: Flighty creature finds berries on the willow

blocks.note: cricket bats are made of willow

explanation.surface: A flighty animal comes across berries growing on a willow tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The willow' is a common nickname for a cricket bat. 'Flighty' looks like fickle but means able to fly.
explanation.definitionFit: Fruit bats are large winged mammals that feed on fruit, so they are flying animals.

clue.text: Bellowed, kind of sneezed, and whistled (Alice): to urge boat to move

definitions.text: Bellowed, kind of sneezed, and whistled (Alice)

indicators.note: the letters are moved about into a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone making odd noises to get a boat going, citing Alice.
explanation.walkthrough: In Through the Looking-Glass, Humpty Dumpty explains to Alice that outgribing is something between bellowing and whistling, with a kind of sneeze in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Lewis Carroll's Jabberwocky has 'the mome raths outgrabe', glossed by Humpty Dumpty as that noise.

clue.text: Shrub with 6 and "I say, a moving grove"

indicators.note: a speaker's phrase, so the grove's name is given by how it is pronounced

blocks.note: Birnam Wood, which comes to Dunsinane in Macbeth

explanation.surface: A garden plant described with a number and a dramatic quotation.
explanation.walkthrough: The witches promise Macbeth safety until Birnam Wood moves to Dunsinane; soldiers carrying its branches make the grove move. '6' looks like a cross-reference but is just the number.
explanation.definitionFit: Viburnum is a genus of flowering shrubs, including guelder rose and laurustinus.

clue.text: Tick over - no good?

blocks.note: first meaning: run an engine slowly without driving anything

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark makes it sound like asking if an engine is faulty; the two parts are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: An engine left running in neutral is said to idle, and idle also means worthless or vain.

clue.text: Homes for bloke in rising water

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means read from bottom to top
the fellow is placed inside the water

explanation.surface: Housing for a man caught in floodwater.
explanation.walkthrough: Bod is British slang for a person or chap.
explanation.definitionFit: Abodes are dwellings, places where people live, so they are homes.

clue.text: Associate goblin with aristocrat

explanation.surface: Keeping company with a goblin and a noble.
explanation.walkthrough: A nob is British slang for a person of high social standing.
explanation.definitionFit: To hobnob is to mix socially, especially with people grander than oneself, so to associate.

clue.text: Union negotiator puts down indicator about one in fury with comrade

indicators.note: the indicator word goes round everything that follows in the clue
the single letter is placed inside the word for anger

blocks.note: a marker is something put down to indicate a place
short for brother, a fellow member

explanation.surface: A trade union official slaps down a gauge in anger with a fellow worker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Union negotiator' sounds like a trade unionist, but the union is a wedding. One goes in fury; that and the comrade go inside the marker.
explanation.definitionFit: A marriage broker arranges matches between couples, bargaining terms for a wedding, a kind of union.

clue.text: See 5
Old tiara bought initially off the back of a lorry

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the purchase word is kept
off as in gone bad or out of order, so the letters are disordered

explanation.surface: An antique tiara picked up cheaply from a dodgy dealer, as stolen goods are said to come off a lorry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Off the back of a lorry' is British slang for stolen goods, which hides both the anagram signal and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A tailboard is the hinged board closing the rear of a truck or cart, which can be let down for loading.

clue.text: Comment of stable relationship among those next door?

definitions.text: Comment of stable relationship among those next door?

blocks.clueFragment: Comment of stable relationship among those next door?
blocks.note: surface reading: remark on how steadily people living next door get on
setter's reading: the noise a horse in a stable makes, which also begins the word for next-door people

explanation.walkthrough: 'Stable relationship' sounds like a settled friendship, but stable means a horse's home; the horse's call is also the first syllable of neighbours.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse's cry is its call, and that sound opens the word for people living next door.

clue.text: Harlot has gold - which is in character? Not quite

indicators.note: falling short means the last letter of the character word is lost
the metal is placed inside the shortened character word

explanation.surface: A prostitute with gold, wondering whether that suits her nature.
explanation.walkthrough: Or is gold in heraldry. 'Character' looks like personality but means a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Lorette was a nineteenth-century French term for a kept woman or courtesan, so a harlot.

clue.text: Theme that has to be mastered

blocks.note: second meaning: one under a ruler's power

explanation.walkthrough: 'Has to be mastered' suggests a topic to learn, but it also describes someone ruled by a sovereign.
explanation.definitionFit: A topic of discussion is a subject, and so is a person owing obedience to a monarch who masters them.
